content: Inhaled corticosteroids are a cornerstone in the treatment of childhood asthma. However, there is significant concern regarding their potential side effects, particularly their impact on growth. It is important to note that asthma itself may contribute to growth retardation. Since growth rates in children are not constant, randomized controlled trials with parallel group designs are necessary to evaluate the effects of inhaled corticosteroids on growth. This review specifically focuses on beclomethasone, an inhaled steroid known for its substantial systemic absorption. The primary objective of this review was to determine whether inhaled beclomethasone significantly delays linear growth in children with asthma. To address this, the Cochrane Airways Group asthma register was searched, and additional references were identified through bibliographies of included studies and existing reviews. Researchers and colleagues in the field of asthma were also contacted to identify relevant trials. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized, controlled trials that compared the effects of beclomethasone to non-steroidal treatments (either placebo or non-steroidal therapy) on the linear growth of children with asthma. Data related to the clinical outcome of change in growth were independently extracted by two reviewers. The search strategy and bibliography review identified 159 citations, of which three studies met the inclusion criteria. All three studies involved children with mild to moderate asthma who were treated with beclomethasone at a dose of 200 mcg twice daily, delivered via a dry powder Diskhaler. The duration of these studies ranged from 7 to 12 months. In all three studies, children treated with beclomethasone experienced a significant reduction in linear growth compared to those receiving placebo or non-steroidal asthma therapy. A meta-analysis of the data revealed an average decrease in growth of -1.54 cm per year (95% confidence interval: -1.15 to -1.94 cm). The authors concluded that in children with mild to moderate asthma, treatment with beclomethasone at a dose of 200 mcg twice daily resulted in a reduction in linear growth of approximately 1.54 cm per year. However, since the studies lasted a maximum of 54 weeks, it remains uncertain whether this growth suppression persists over time or if there is a compensatory catch-up growth after discontinuation of therapy. The review does not provide information on the growth effects of other inhaled corticosteroids that may have lower systemic absorption. For children requiring inhaled corticosteroids to manage asthma, it is recommended to use the lowest effective dose to control symptoms and to closely monitor the child’s growth.
